entries.content:
GLM-5.3-Flash combines linear and sparse attention, a mixture-of-experts design, and manifold constrained hyperconnections. A scaled-down version with 25 million parameters can be built in Python and trained on a standard CPU.

We just published a course on the freeCodeCamp.org YouTube channel that will teach you how to build and train a multimodal language model from scratch, covering both pre-training and post-training. The course is from @vukrosic, and all of the code, slides, and experiments are in the GitHub repository linked in the video description.

The model uses a 260-token byte-level vocabulary, a 192-token context, and a small vision encoder that turns a 32 by 32 image into 16 tokens.

In this course, you will learn:

  • Tokenization & Embeddings

    Why a small model needs a small byte-level vocabulary and how weight tying shares one matrix between the embeddings and the output head.
  • Linear & Sparse Attention

    How linear attention keeps a fixed-size memory of recent tokens while every fourth layer uses sparse attention with an indexer to find distant details.
  • Mixture of Experts

    How tokens are routed to a few chosen experts plus a shared expert that learns information common to every token.
  • Adding Vision

    How images are split into patches with 2D RoPE and merged into image tokens so the model can recognize digits.
  • Pre-Training Experiments

    How data diversity, interleaving, and curriculums affect learning, including how interleaving helps prevent catastrophic forgetting.
  • Reinforcement Learning

    How to design reward functions, compute advantages as in GRPO, update only the final layers, and test group size, temperature, and seeds.

After reinforcement learning, the model goes from solving 0 of 24 Python tasks to 16 of 24.

Watch the full course on the freeCodeCamp.org YouTube channel (44-minute watch).

entries.title: How to Speed Up CI in the Age of AI-Written Code
entries.summary: Coding agents now write code faster than most CI pipelines can check it. In April 2026, GitHub COO Kyle Daigle said that his platform was handling 275 million commits a week, on pace for 14 billion in
entries.content:
Coding agents now write code faster than most CI pipelines can check it. In April 2026, GitHub COO Kyle Daigle said that his platform was handling 275 million commits a week, on pace for 14 billion in the year, up from about 1 billion in 2025. In the same post, he put GitHub Actions at 2.1 billion minutes in a single week, up from 500 million a week in 2023.

That second figure shows where all those commits end up: in CI. A 15-minute pipeline is tolerable if a dev pushes a few times a day. When an agent opens ten PRs in an afternoon, that pipeline turns into a queue. You wait for results, agents wait to retry, and the time saved writing code is lost checking it.

Most of that delay comes from a few causes, and each has a known fix. You can speed up CI in five ways:

  • measure where the time goes
  • cache what you can reuse
  • run jobs on faster hardware
  • split tests across parallel jobs
  • skip work that doesn't need to run.

In this article, we'll walk through each fix in order. You’ll learn how to find the slowest steps in your GitHub Actions workflows, cache dependencies and Docker layers with stable keys, and move heavy jobs to faster runners. You’ll also see how to shard tests across a matrix of parallel jobs, and how to skip unneeded work with path filters, affected-only tests, and concurrency groups.

What We'll Cover:

Measure First, Then Optimize

Most teams try to guess which step is slowing things down, and they're often wrong. A job that feels like a test problem may be 90 seconds of installs and 30 seconds of tests.

Start with data you already have. GitHub shows job execution time for every run, with a timing for each step. Open the last ten runs of your slowest workflow and note the three longest steps. Use the median, not the worst case, since one slow run can be a network blip.

Also separate waiting from working. Queue time, setup time, and run time need different fixes. If jobs sit in a queue for a minute, no test tuning will help.

Cache Dependencies and Build Layers

The fastest work is work you never repeat. Every run starts on a fresh machine, so without a cache you download the same packages again and again.

The dependency caching reference explains how 

actions/cache
works. You give it a path and a key. If the key matches a saved cache, the files are restored. If not, the step runs, and the files are saved when the job ends.

Everything depends on that key. The usual pattern hashes your lockfile, so the key changes only when your dependencies change.

- uses: actions/cache@v6
  with:
    path: ~/.npm
    # Key changes only when the lockfile changes
    key: npm-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}
    restore-keys: |
      npm-${{ runner.os }}-

The 

restore-keys
line is the part that tends to get skipped. When the exact key misses, it restores the closest older cache. You still install a few new packages, but not all of them. Be careful with keys that include a timestamp or a commit SHA. Those never match twice, so you save a new cache on every run and never reuse one.

Docker builds need the same thinking. Docker images are built in layers, and a layer is reused only if everything above it is unchanged. Copy your lockfile and install dependencies first, then copy your source code. That way a code change doesn't rebuild the install layer. To keep layers between runs, point BuildKit at the GitHub Actions cache backend with 

cache-from
and 
cache-to
set to 
type=gha
.

One catch is that these caches live in remote storage. Each restore is a network download, which on a big cache can rival the install it replaces.

Run on Faster Hardware

Caching avoids repeating work. This improvement is different. It runs the work itself on faster machines.

Standard GitHub-hosted runners for private repositories have 2 vCPUs and 7 GB of RAM. Avrea is a drop-in replacement for GitHub Actions runners. You change one line, from 

runs-on: ubuntu-latest
to an Avrea label such as 
runs-on: avrea-ubuntu-latest
, and the rest of your workflow stays the same. By Avrea's own numbers, jobs run about 2x faster on hardware alone, and up to 10x faster with cache hits.

Independent numbers point the same way. RunsOn maintains a public runner benchmark that builds three open-source projects on nine runner services with build caches turned off: a Rust test suite, TypeScript typechecks, and a production Docker build of PostHog. In the 4-vCPU x64 category, as of November 2026, Avrea finished all three in about 7 minutes of build time, compared with about 18.5 minutes on GitHub's 4-core runner, not counting runner start-up.

Built-in caching is the other half, and it connects to the section above. Avrea keeps its caches in the same datacenter as its runners, so a restore doesn't cross a slow network. Most of it is pre-configured.

The GitHub Actions cache and package downloads for npm, pip, Go modules, and Cargo work with no workflow changes. Build caches for tools such as Go, Bazel, Gradle, Turborepo, Nx, and sccache are set up on the runner, and some need a small workflow addition. So a team gets cache hits without writing key logic for each tool.

Other providers take other routes. Depot offers faster GitHub Actions runners and remote Docker builds, and now runs its own CI engine that accepts GitHub Actions workflows. RunsOn is self-hosted: it starts EC2 instances inside your own AWS account, so you pay AWS for compute plus a flat yearly license, instead of a per-minute fee to RunsOn. GitHub's own larger runners, available on Team and Enterprise Cloud plans, add more CPU, RAM, and disk, plus options like static IPs and GPUs, billed by the minute. Check each provider's site for current details, since all of them change often.

Parallelize and Shard Your Tests

Once each job is fast, make sure jobs don't wait in a line. A long test suite on one runner is the classic bottleneck.

Start with independent jobs. Lint, type checks, unit tests, and build rarely need each other. GitHub runs jobs in parallel unless you add 

needs
, so remove any 
needs
line that's only there for habit.

Next, use a matrix. A matrix strategy creates one job per combination of values, and they all run at once. Teams often use it for Node versions, but it's also the simplest way to shard tests.

strategy:
  fail-fast: false
  matrix:
    shard: [1, 2, 3, 4]
steps:
  # Each job runs one quarter of the suite
  - run: npx jest --shard=${{ matrix.shard }}/4

Jest's 

--shard
flag splits the suite across jobs by test file. Four shards can turn a twelve-minute suite into about three, plus setup time, if the files take similar time. If a few files are much heavier, one shard will run long, so split those files up. Setting 
fail-fast: false
lets every shard finish, so you see all failures at once.

Playwright works the same way. Run 

npx playwright test --shard=1/4
in each matrix job, then merge the reports at the end.

Sharding has a limit. Each shard pays its own setup cost, so past a point more shards add cost without saving time. Inside a single job, tools like pytest-xdist spread tests across the CPUs on the machine.

Do Less Work on Every Run

The last one is the cheapest: don't run what you don't need to run.

Path filters are the easiest start. In the workflow syntax, the 

paths
and 
paths-ignore
keys let a workflow run only when certain files change. A change to the docs folder shouldn't trigger a full backend build.

One warning: if a required status check never runs because of a path filter, the pull request stays stuck on a pending check. For required checks, let the workflow run and skip the job with an 

if:
condition instead, since GitHub counts a skipped job as passed.

In a monorepo, go further and run only affected tests. Tools such as Nx, Turborepo, and Bazel work out which packages a change touches and skip the rest. In Nx that's 

nx affected -t test
, and in Turborepo it's 
turbo run test --affected
. Both compare your branch against 
main
, so check out enough Git history for that comparison, since 
actions/checkout
fetches a single commit by default.

Most commits touch a small part of a large codebase, so the savings add up. This matters more when agents open many small pull requests, each touching a package or two.

Finally, stop paying for runs that no one needs. When you push twice in a row, the first run is already out of date. A concurrency group cancels it.

concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  # Cancel the older run when a new push arrives
  cancel-in-progress: true

This matters more as AI tools push more commits. Agents may update a branch many times an hour, and each push starts a full run. Don't use it on deploy workflows, though. Cancelling a deploy halfway can leave a bad state, so queue those instead.

Putting It Together

Measure first, because that shows which of the other four fixes is worth your time. Cache with stable keys and order your Dockerfile so slow layers stay put. Move heavy jobs to faster runners, and compare providers on your own workflow. Shard tests until setup time dominates. Then cut needless work with path filters, affected-only tests, and cancelled stale runs.

Make one change at a time and re-check your timings after each. Saving two minutes on a job that runs fifty times a day beats a clever fix on a job that runs once.

Hope you enjoyed this article. You can connect with me on LinkedIn.

entries.title: Schema Drift vs. Semantic Drift in Data Pipelines
entries.summary: When a column is removed from a source database or dataset, the next pipeline run usually fails, making the problem easy to detect. But when a field keeps the same name and data type but its meaning c
entries.content:
When a column is removed from a source database or dataset, the next pipeline run usually fails, making the problem easy to detect. But when a field keeps the same name and data type but its meaning changes (known as semantic drift), the pipeline can continue running normally, allowing the problem to go unnoticed.

This happens because a schema describes the structure of data, not what the values actually represent. It tells us which fields exist, their data types, and whether they can contain null values, but not whether a timestamp uses UTC, a durability score should range from 10 to 100, or an empty string means something different from null.

As a result, most pipeline checks are designed to catch obvious errors, such as missing columns or incorrect data types, but often fail to detect less obvious problems where the data looks correct but its meaning or values have changed.

I wanted to see how far this limitation reaches in practice, so I built a small lab where I introduced nine types of pipeline failures and tested four detectors against each one. This article looks at what each detector caught and what happened when changes went unnoticed and corrupted the data.

You can find the code here and reproduce the experiment with a few commands.

What We'll Cover:

Prerequisites

To follow along and run the lab yourself, you’ll need:

  • Python 3.10 or newer, and basic comfort reading Python code
  • Pydantic v2, installed with 
    pip install pydantic
  • Git, to clone the repository
  • A terminal, to run the scripts
  • Basic SQL, such as 
    GROUP BY
    and 
    WHERE ... IS NULL
    . SQLite comes with Python, so there is nothing extra to install.
  • A general idea of what a data pipeline does: reading data from a source, transforming it, and loading it somewhere else

How the Lab Works

I intentionally kept the pipeline simple. It reads 1,000 game-inventory records from a JSONL file, flattens the nested 

stats
and 
attributes
objects, loads the data into SQLite, and calculates six metrics: total number of records, unequipped items, item counts by rarity, average attack per category, items acquired per day, and average durability. I also left out defensive checks so that each change could affect the pipeline in the same way it might affect a real pipeline when someone assumes the source data is reliable.

Each drift applies a deterministic function that takes one record and returns a changed one, so every result is repeatable. For instance, the timezone drift shifts each UTC timestamp to UTC+4 wall time and drops the offset:

def local_time_without_offset(row):
    timestamp = row["acquired_at"]
    if not timestamp.endswith("Z"):
        raise ValueError(f"Expected UTC timestamp ending in Z, got: {timestamp!r}")

    utc_time = datetime.fromisoformat(timestamp.removesuffix("Z") + "+00:00")
    local_time = utc_time + timedelta(hours=4)
    row["acquired_at"] = local_time.replace(tzinfo=None).isoformat()
    return row

After applying each drift, I ran the pipeline and saved its output in a separate SQLite database. I then compared it with the database generated from the original data, checking each row and column for differences. This step helped identify whether the pipeline had produced correct results, rather than simply checking whether it ran successfully.

The comparison placed each change into one of four categories:

  • failed loudly (the error names a field the drift touched)
  • failed confusingly (the pipeline crashed but the error doesn't mention the cause)
  • passed with corruption (it finished, but values differ from the baseline)
  • or passed clean (the database matches the baseline exactly).

I tested each drifted file with four detectors. Each detector follows the same structure: it takes the baseline file and the incoming file as input, checks for changes, and returns whether it found a problem along with a message. This shared interface keeps the setup simple and makes it easy to add more detectors.

The four detectors are:

  • Schema snapshot diff: Compares the fields and data types in the incoming file against the baseline to identify schema changes.
  • Loose Pydantic model: Validates the data against a basic set of rules and restricts 
    rarity
    to the five known values.
  • Strict Pydantic model: Applies additional validation rules. It also restricts 
    rarity
    to the five known values, requires timezone-aware timestamps, limits 
    equipped_slot
    to five known values, and rejects unknown top-level fields. This refers to the validation rules in the model, not Pydantic's 
    strict=True
    mode.
  • Statistical profile: Compares the statistical profile of the incoming data with the baseline. It checks each field's mean, category shares, and null rate to identify changes that the other detectors might miss

Understanding Data Shape and Meaning

The rest of this article uses two terms: data shape and data meaning. Data shape refers to the fields in a dataset, their paths, and the types of values they contain. The schema detector captures this information by checking each field and the types found in it.

def walk(obj, prefix, schema):
    for key, value in obj.items():
        field = f"{prefix}{key}"
        if isinstance(value, dict):
            walk(value, field + ".", schema)
        else:
            schema.setdefault(field, set()).add(type(value).__name__)

For the baseline, this returns entries like 

acquired_at: {'str'}
, 
equipped_slot: {'NoneType', 'str'}
, and 
attributes.durability: {'int'}
.

Data meaning, however, includes everything the dictionary leaves out including the unit and time zone of a value, its expected range, the set of valid strings, and what a null value represents. This reveals a limitation of any detector that only looks at data shape. Since the schema detector bases its results on the dictionary of field paths and data types, it can't distinguish between datasets that produce the same dictionary but contain values with different meanings.

Three of the nine drifts left this dictionary unchanged: the timezone shift, the new enum value, and the durability scaling. As a result, the schema detector didn't flag any of them.

Detectors can check data at different levels:

  • Shape: Checks which fields exist and the types of values they contain.
  • Value constraints: Checks whether individual values follow specific rules, such as requiring timezone information or limiting a field to a known set of values.
  • Distribution: Compares statistics, such as averages, category shares, and null rates, against a baseline. This can reveal changes in the data without defining exactly what each value should mean.
  • Semantics: Checks what the data actually represents, including units, timezone conventions, and the meaning of null values. These rules require knowledge of the data and must come from the people or systems that produce and use it.

The four detectors cover the first three levels. The fourth level goes beyond what these detectors can establish because a dataset can pass checks on its structure, individual values, and statistical distributions while its meaning has changed. To know what the data means, we need context that can't be gotten from its values alone.

The Results Matrix

The results matrix summarizes how each of the four detectors responded to the nine drift scenarios.

for drift in ALL_DRIFTS:
    dst = ROOT / "data" / "drifted" / f"{drift.name}.jsonl"
    drifted_db = DB_DIR / f"{drift.name}.db"

    apply_drift(drift, BASELINE, dst)
    result = run_pipeline(dst, db_path=str(drifted_db))
    outcome = classify(result, baseline_db, drifted_db, drift.fields)

    detected = {
        det.name: det.check(str(BASELINE), str(dst))["detected"]
        for det in DETECTORS
    }

    rows.append((drift, outcome, detected, result.get("error")))

It shows which changes they caught, which they missed, and whether the pipeline failed or continued with incorrect data.

"Yes (only)” means that detector was the only one to catch the change. “n/a” means the pipeline crashed, so no rows were loaded.

Pipeline Errors

The strict model detected the most changes (7 out of 9), followed by the schema diff (6), the loose model (4), and the statistical profile (2).

But each detector missed some changes. Three drifts were detected by only one detector: the strict model caught the timezone shift, the schema diff caught the 

level
change, and the statistical profile caught the durability scaling.

Detecting Changes in Data Shape

Five of the nine drifts changed the data structure. These included renaming 

rarity
, removing 
equipped_slot
, adding a 
guild
field, replacing the 
stats
object with an array, and changing 
level
from an integer to a string.

The schema diff detected all five changes. The strict model detected four, and the loose model detected three. This shows that the schema diff was the most effective at detecting structural changes.

The pipeline failed on three of the drifts, but some error messages were more useful than others. Renaming 

rarity
caused a 
KeyError: 'rarity'
, which tells us exactly which field is missing. Replacing 
stats
with 
[attack, defense, speed]
caused a 
TypeError: list indices must be integers or slices, not str
. This message explains the type of error but doesn't identify the field involved. To find the cause, the reader has to trace the error back through the transformation code.

The classifier labels the first error loud and the second confusing.It makes this distinction by checking whether the error message mentions a field affected by the drift.

if result["status"] == "error":
    error_text = result["error"].lower()
    names_cause = any(f.lower() in error_text for f in drift_fields)
    return {
        "label": "failed_loudly" if names_cause else "failed_confusingly",
        "rows_affected": None,
        "loss_cells": 0,
        "corrupt_cells": 0,
        "extra_rows": 0,
    }

The Pydantic detectors ran on the same file and reported 

stats: Input should be a valid dictionary
, directly identifying the field with the problem.

The 

level
change reveals another way a structural change can go undetected. Both Pydantic models accepted it because Pydantic's default lax mode converts the string 
"42"
into the integer 
42
. The pipeline also accepted it because SQLite's INTEGER affinity converts text that looks like a number when inserting it into an INTEGER column. As a result, the database matched the baseline, and the classifier labeled the run 
passed_clean
.

Only the schema diff detected the change because it checks the type of the raw value before any conversion takes place. This shows the limitation of checking data after coercion: once a value has been converted, the original type change is no longer visible. In this case, the simplest detector caught a change that both Pydantic models accepted.

The experiment also showed that not every detected change causes a problem. Adding 

guild
and changing 
level
from an integer to a string both triggered alerts. The schema diff detected both changes, while the strict model detected only the addition of 
guild
. But neither change corrupted any rows because the load step reads only the fields it expects.

This highlights the need to distinguish between changes that should stop a pipeline and those that only need to be logged. If detectors flag too many harmless changes, users may start to ignore their warnings.

Semantic Changes: What the Wrong Numbers Looked Like

The remaining drifts didn't change the fields or data types. They changed what the values represented. These changes were harder to detect but had real effects on the results. The table below shows the impact of each drift and whether it was visible in the pipeline's output.

DriftRows corruptedMetric that movedBeforeAfter
Timestamps shifted to UTC+4, offset dropped1,000items acquired per dayJan 2: 9, Jan 3: 3Jan 2: 6, Jan 3: 6
Null slots replaced with 
""

mythic
rarity on 20 rows		 20item count per raritycommon: 619common: 609, mythic: 20
Durability multiplied by 101,000average durability54.78547.85

A major thing I noticed is that most of the numbers still look normal. For example, moving timestamps forward by four hours shifts some items onto the next calendar day. Since four hours is one-sixth of a day, roughly one in six items moves to a different day. Each day loses some items to the next day but also gains items from the previous day.

The total number of items remains 1,000, and the daily counts change very little overall. With an average of about 5.5 items per day, the counts already vary by two or three items. So a drop from 9 items to 6 can easily look like typical variation rather than a data problem.

The pipeline's total-row-count check still passed because no items were lost. Any check that only compares totals would also miss the problem. The total is correct, but some items are now counted under the wrong day.

I also looked at why the pipeline didn't report a problem. The original timestamp, 

2026-01-02T22:30:00+00:00
, changed to 
2026-01-03T02:30:00
after the drift. The new timestamp has no timezone offset, so 
datetime.fromisoformat
reads it as a naïve datetime. The 
isoformat()
method then writes it back without an offset. SQLite's 
DATE()
treats this offset-free timestamp as UTC, placing the item on January 3 instead of January 2.

The pipeline processed the timestamp without errors but assigned the item to the wrong day. If the producer had written 

2026-01-03T02:30:00+04:00
instead, the timestamp would have represented the same instant as the original. SQLite would have converted it to UTC, and the item would still have been counted on January 2.

The problem was the missing timezone offset. Without it, the pipeline had no way to know which timezone the timestamp represented, so it treated the time as UTC.

The empty-string drift caused a different problem. Replacing 

null
with 
""
kept the field as a string, so checks that only verify the data type still passed.

The schema diff caught the change because the type set for 

equipped_slot
changed from 
{'NoneType', 'str'}
to 
{'str'}
. The pipeline raised no errors, but the query 
WHERE equipped_slot IS NULL
returned no rows. The dashboard would show 0 unequipped items instead of 205, making it look as though every player had equipped their gear.

The statistical profile showed what had happened: 

equipped_slot: null rate 20% -> 0%; equipped_slot='': share 0% -> 20%
. The null values had been replaced with empty strings, not real values.

The new 

mythic
rarity went through the pipeline without an error for a similar reason. The drift changed 20 records to 
mythic
: 10 from 
common
(619 to 609), 9 from 
uncommon
(236 to 227), and 1 from 
rare
(98 to 97). The query 
GROUP BY rarity
accepted the new value without any error. It simply created a new row for 
mythic
and reduced the counts for the other rarities. A dashboard that only knows the five original rarities might hide 
mythic
or group it under "other", depending on how it handles unknown values.

The durability change shows most clearly how data can keep the same structure but mean something different. In the original data, durability ranges from 10 to 100, so an average of 547.85 is clearly wrong. But the field kept the same name and integer type, so the schema diff didn't detect the change.

The pipeline also accepted the values because nothing checked them against the expected range. Only a check that knows durability should be between 10 and 100 can catch this problem. To test this, I added a range constraint to the strict Pydantic model:

class RangedAttributes(Attributes):
    durability: int = Field(ge=10, le=100)


class StrictWithRange(StrictItem):
    attributes: RangedAttributes


flagged = 0
for row in drifted:
    try:
        StrictWithRange(**row)
    except ValidationError:
        flagged += 1

This caught 985 of the 1,000 drifted records. The remaining 15 had an original durability value of 10, which became 100 after scaling by 10. Since 100 still falls within the allowed range, those records passed validation.

Damage vs. Visibility

The four drifts corrupted 1,000, 205, 20, and 1,000 rows, but each one changed only one of the six metrics the pipeline calculates. The other five metrics stayed the same. Anyone monitoring the pipeline could miss the damage unless they checked the affected metric and knew its expected value.

The main finding is that data can change across many rows without changing most of the results people monitor. People only notice the problem if they check the metric that the drift affects.

Detecting Changes in Data Meaning

To catch changes beyond the data structure, we need checks that examine the values themselves.

The strict model checks whether values follow specific rules. It caught the timezone drift because 

AwareDatetime
rejects timestamps without a timezone offset (
acquired_at: Input should have timezone info
). It also caught the empty-string slot because its 
Literal
rule only accepts five known slot names and rejects 
""
.

The loose model has fewer restrictions. It accepts any string for 

acquired_at
, any string or 
None
for 
equipped_slot
, and unknown fields. As a result, it missed the timezone shift, the empty-string slot, and the new column.

The strict model also missed the durability change because I hadn't defined an allowed range for that field. In a separate run, I added 

Field(ge=10, le=100)
to a copy of the model. This caught 985 of the 1,000 changed rows. It missed the remaining 15 because their original durability was 10, which became exactly 100 after scaling and still passed the check.

The statistical profile compares data distributions with the baseline. It was the only detector to catch the durability scaling because it doesn't need a predefined range. It simply detected that the average durability rose from 54.8 to 547.9.

But it may also flag normal changes in the data. To test this, I scaled durability by factors from 1.02 to 1.3 and tried four mean-change thresholds. I also tested the detector on 200 clean files generated with different seeds to see how often it raised false alarms. I excluded the baseline seed because it would produce identical data.

Mean thresholdFalse alarms, durability onlyFalse alarms, any numeric fieldShifts caught
25%0 / 2000 / 2001.3x only
10%0 / 2000 / 2001.1x and above
5%0 / 20023 / 200 (11.5%)1.05x and above
2%37 / 200 (18.5%)188 / 200 (94%)every shift tested

The 2% threshold shows how easily the detector can flag normal variation. Durability is roughly uniform from 10 to 100, so a 1,000-row sample has a standard deviation of about 26. That means the sample mean typically lands within about 0.8 of the true mean, which is roughly 1.5% of its value. A 2% threshold is only a little bigger than that, so it should fire on roughly 18% of clean files. It fired on 37 of 200 (18.5%). This shows a tradeoff that lowering the threshold helps catch small changes but also increases false alarms.

The results also show why one threshold doesn't work for every numeric field. 

stats.attack
, 
level
, and 
player_id
vary more than durability relative to their averages. At a 2% threshold, at least one of these fields triggered an alarm in 188 of 200 clean files. At 5%, they caused all 23 false alarms, while durability caused none. 
stats.attack
caused 15 of those alarms. Even 
player_id
triggered alarms, although its average has no useful meaning.

Using a single threshold treats every numeric field the same, even though some vary more than others and some shouldn't be checked by their average at all.

The category-share check uses a fixed 5-percentage-point threshold, so changing the mean threshold doesn't affect its results. It raised 26 alarms across 22 of the 200 clean files (11%). Seventeen alarms involved 

equipped_slot
, and 16 of those involved 
chest
or 
off_hand
.

There are two reasons for these alarms. First, the check calculates each slot's share using only the 795 non-null rows, not all 1,000. This gives each share a standard error of about 1.4 percentage points.

Second, my baseline doesn't match the intended shares exactly. 

chest
makes up 17.2% of the baseline instead of the intended 20%. As a result, a clean file only needs to reach 22.2% to trigger an alarm. This happens in roughly 6% of files. 
off_hand
has the opposite problem: its baseline share is higher than intended, at 22.3%. This shows that a baseline can contain its own sampling errors, which then affect every comparison.

One more limitation comes from the detector design, not from a measured result. I didn't test this case, but the code shows why it would go undetected. The strict model caught the timezone drift because the timestamp lost its offset. But a producer could shift the clock and keep the 

Z
suffix. Every detector would then accept the data. The strict model checks only whether a timestamp has an offset, not whether the time is correct. The statistical profile skips timestamp strings because they have too many distinct values to treat as categories and aren't numeric.

This is a limitation of the fourth layer: the timestamp still looks valid, but it represents the wrong time. None of the detectors checks whether the timestamp matches the actual time it is supposed to represent.

What this Experiment Suggests

The results suggest that combining all four detectors provides better coverage because each one catches changes the others miss.

The schema diff is simple and cheap to run on every load. It caught six of the nine drifts, including the 

level
change that both Pydantic models missed because they converted the value before checking it. It also identified the field that caused an error when the pipeline's own error message did not. But it caught only one of the four drifts that corrupted data.

The strict model and statistical profile caught all four harmful drifts between them. I'd use the strict model for fields with known rules, such as timezone-aware timestamps, allowed values, and numeric ranges. I'd use statistical checks for important metrics that have no clear validation rules, setting a separate threshold for each field based on past data.

The lab showed why one threshold doesn't work for every field. A global 5% mean threshold raised 23 false alarms across 200 clean files, all from fields other than durability. I'd only apply statistical checks to fields where the average is meaningful and set thresholds based on how much each field normally varies.

The fourth layer requires the producer and consumers to agree on what the data means. If the producer changes a field's unit, time zone, or allowed values without telling anyone, consumers can't interpret it correctly. Both sides should agree on clear rules, such as the unit of measurement, the time zone, and the allowed values.

This is a recommendation based on what my detectors couldn't catch. I haven't tested this approach in the lab yet.

Limitations

The data is synthetic and independent, so it's much simpler than real data, which often has seasonal patterns and natural growth. Real-world false-alarm rates may therefore be higher than the ones I measured. I also used one fixed baseline, so any sampling error in that sample affects every comparison. A production system would likely use a rolling baseline instead.

I used the same thresholds across fields. Setting a separate threshold based on how much each field normally varies might work better, but I didn't test this. I also tested only four detectors from a much larger set of available tools. These results show where the detectors have blind spots, not which tools are best.

Finally, I chose to group changes into "shape" and "meaning," but some changes, such as replacing 

null
with an empty string, could fit into either group.

My first threshold test also contained a bug. I used the wrong variable name (

SEED
instead of 
seed
) in the data generator, which caused all 20 clean files to match the baseline exactly. This produced zero false alarms. A result that good at a 2% threshold seemed unlikely, so I checked the code and found the mistake. I corrected the bug and excluded seed 42, the baseline's own seed, because it would generate identical data and could never trigger an alarm. All results in this article use the corrected run.

Conclusion

The experiment showed that schema changes are not the only source of pipeline failures. The schema diff caught all five structural changes but missed semantic changes that left field names and types untouched. For example, timestamps shifted to the wrong day, null values became empty strings, and durability values increased tenfold. In each case, the pipeline ran successfully but produced incorrect results.

The four detectors caught different types of changes, and using them together improved detection coverage. However, detecting changes is only part of the problem. Pipeline checks also need to validate whether values fall within expected ranges and whether they still represent what downstream calculations assume.

A pipeline completing successfully doesn't necessarily mean the data is correct. It’s just as important to check that the data retains its intended meaning and that downstream calculations still produce reliable results.

entries.content:
Before anyone films a video, shoots an ad or draws the final pages of a comic, someone usually sketches the plan as a storyboard: one picture per shot, in order, with a short note about what happens and how long it lasts.

Most people already have those pictures. They are phone photos, screenshots, rough sketches or AI-generated frames sitting in a folder. What they don't have is a quick way to turn that folder into clean, numbered sheets they can print or send to a client.

In this tutorial, you'll build a browser-based tool that does exactly that. You'll add a set of images, give each one a title, a description and a duration, choose a layout, preview the sheets, and download a print-ready PDF.

Everything runs in the browser. The images are never uploaded to a server, which matters when the frames are unreleased product shots or client work.

Along the way, you'll learn how to fix sideways phone photos, sort files the way people expect, lay out a page in PDF points, wrap text on a canvas, save a draft with IndexedDB, and build a PDF that keeps photos sharp without making the file huge.

I built this tool for AllInOneTools, where it runs as the Image Storyboard to PDF tool. This article walks through a simplified version that you can build in three files.

What We'll Cover

What This Image Storyboard Tool Does and How It Works

The tool takes a list of images and turns them into storyboard sheets. Each image becomes a frame with:

  • a label, such as 
    Shot 1
    or 
    Scene 1
  • an optional title
  • a description of what happens
  • an optional duration in seconds

The frames are placed on sheets in one of four layouts:

  • One frame per page, for presenting each shot large
  • Grid, for seeing the whole sequence at a glance
  • Panels with notes, with ruled lines for handwritten notes on set
  • Film strip, with sprocket holes for a classic look

Each sheet has a title, the total running time and a sheet number at the top.

Here's the flow from start to finish:

Images → frames (title, description, duration)
       → layout (where each box goes, in PDF points)
       → canvas (labels, text, lines)
       → PDF (photos as JPEG + one text layer per sheet)
       → download

Why the Text Is Drawn on a Canvas

PDF-lib can write real text into a PDF, but only with a font file you embed. The standard PDF fonts only cover basic Latin characters, so a description in Hindi, Gujarati, Arabic or Japanese would fail.

A canvas, on the other hand, can draw any text the device can show, using the fonts the device already has. So this tool draws all the text on a canvas at 300 dpi and puts that canvas into the PDF as an image.

The trade-off is that the text in the PDF isn't selectable or searchable. For a storyboard, which is mostly printed and looked at, that's usually fine. If you need searchable text, you'd embed a font with PDF-lib's 

fontkit
support instead.

Project Setup

You need only three files:

image-storyboard/
├── index.html
├── style.css
└── script.js

Open 

index.html
through a local server (for example, the Live Server extension in VS Code) rather than as a 
file://
page, so that IndexedDB and downloads behave the same way they will on a real site.

Libraries and Browser APIs Used

This project uses one library and a few built-in browser APIs:

  • PDF-lib creates the PDF, embeds the JPEG and PNG images, and saves the file.
  • Canvas API draws the sheets for the preview and the text layer of the PDF.
  • createImageBitmap
    decodes images and applies the rotation stored in phone photos.
  • IndexedDB keeps a draft in the browser so the work survives a page reload.

You don't need PDF.js here, because there's no PDF to read. Everything starts from images.

Add PDF-lib with a pinned version at the end of the 

body
, before your own script:

Pinning the version means a future release of the library can't break your tool without you knowing.

Creating the HTML Layout

The page has four parts:

  • An upload area with a file input
  • A bar that offers to restore a saved draft
  • A frames panel with one card per image
  • A settings panel and a preview panel

Here's the upload area and the draft bar:




  
Drop images here or

The file input only accepts the formats every browser can decode: JPEG, PNG, WebP and GIF.

The workspace holds the three panels:




  

    

      
Frames

    The settings panel is a list of 

    select
    and 
    number
    inputs. Each one has an 
    id
    that matches a key in the settings object you'll create in JavaScript:
    
  
    Board settings

    The preview panel has the canvas, the sheet navigation and the download controls:

    
  
    Preview

    In 

    style.css
    , add one rule that's easy to forget:
    [hidden] { display: none !important; }

    The workspace uses 

    display: grid
    and the draft bar uses 
    display: flex
    . Those rules are more specific than the browser's default style for the 
    hidden
    attribute, so without this line, hidden elements would still show.

    Selecting the Main Elements

    At the top of 

    script.js
    , set up the constants, the state and the element references:
    // ---------- Constants ----------
const PAPERS = {
  a4: [595.28, 841.89],
  letter: [612, 792],
  a3: [841.89, 1190.55],
  slide: [405, 720],
};
const FONTS = {
  sans: "Arial, Helvetica, 'Noto Sans', sans-serif",
  serif: "Georgia, 'Times New Roman', 'Noto Serif', serif",
  mono: "'Courier New', Courier, monospace",
};
const THUMB_SIZE = 1000;
const ACCEPTED = ['image/jpeg', 'image/png', 'image/webp', 'image/gif'];

// ---------- State ----------
const state = {
  frames: [],
  title: '',
  sheet: 0,
  nextId: 1,
  lastDeleted: null,
  opts: {
    layout: 'grid', cols: 3, rows: 2, paper: 'a4', orient: 'landscape',
    label: 'shot', font: 'sans', textSize: 'm', lines: 3,
  },
};

// ---------- Elements ----------
const $ = (id) => document.getElementById(id);
const els = {
  uploadArea: $('uploadArea'), fileInput: $('fileInput'), selectBtn: $('selectBtn'),
  statusText: $('statusText'), workspace: $('workspace'), frameList: $('frameList'),
  totalTime: $('totalTime'), boardTitle: $('boardTitle'), undoBtn: $('undoBtn'),
  addMoreBtn: $('addMoreBtn'), canvas: $('previewCanvas'), prevBtn: $('prevBtn'),
  nextBtn: $('nextBtn'), sheetInfo: $('sheetInfo'), fileName: $('fileName'),
  quality: $('quality'), downloadBtn: $('downloadBtn'), resetBtn: $('resetBtn'),
  resultText: $('resultText'), draftBar: $('draftBar'), draftText: $('draftText'),
  restoreBtn: $('restoreBtn'), discardBtn: $('discardBtn'),
};
const SETTING_IDS = ['layout', 'cols', 'rows', 'paper', 'orient', 'label', 'font', 'textSize', 'lines'];

    The 

    state
    object is the single source of truth. The frame list, the preview and the PDF are all built from it, which keeps them in sync.

    The paper sizes are in PDF points. One point is 1/72 of an inch, so an A4 page is 595.28 × 841.89 points. You'll do all layout math in points and only convert to pixels when drawing.

    Adding and Loading Images

    Opening Files from the Button or by Dropping Them

    The "Select images" button opens the hidden file input, and dropping files anywhere on the page adds them too:

    // ---------- Upload area ----------
els.selectBtn.addEventListener('click', () => els.fileInput.click());
els.addMoreBtn.addEventListener('click', () => els.fileInput.click());
els.fileInput.addEventListener('change', () => {
  addFiles(els.fileInput.files);
  els.fileInput.value = '';
});

['dragenter', 'dragover'].forEach((type) => {
  document.addEventListener(type, (e) => {
    if (!e.dataTransfer.types.includes('Files')) return;
    e.preventDefault();
    els.uploadArea.classList.add('dragover');
  });
});
['dragleave', 'drop'].forEach((type) => {
  document.addEventListener(type, () => els.uploadArea.classList.remove('dragover'));
});
document.addEventListener('drop', (e) => {
  if (!e.dataTransfer.files.length) return;
  e.preventDefault();
  addFiles(e.dataTransfer.files);
});

function showWorkspace() {
  els.uploadArea.hidden = true;
  els.draftBar.hidden = true;
  els.workspace.hidden = false;
}

    Resetting 

    fileInput.value
    after each pick lets the user choose the same file again later. The 
    dataTransfer.types.includes('Files')
    check makes sure the drop highlight only appears for files, not for frames being dragged inside the list.

    Fixing Phone Photo Rotation

    Phones don't rotate the pixels when you hold them sideways. They save the image in the sensor's orientation and add an EXIF tag that says "rotate this 90° when you show it."

    If you draw such a photo on a canvas with an 

    img
    element in some browsers, or read its width and height before the rotation is applied, the frame comes out sideways or with the wrong shape.

    createImageBitmap
    with 
    imageOrientation: 'from-image'
    asks the browser to apply the EXIF rotation while decoding:
    // ---------- Loading images ----------
// Phone photos store their rotation in EXIF. imageOrientation: 'from-image'
// asks the browser to apply it, so the picture comes out the right way up.
function decodeImage(blob) {
  if ('createImageBitmap' in window) {
    return createImageBitmap(blob, { imageOrientation: 'from-image' })
      .catch(() => loadWithImgTag(blob));
  }
  return loadWithImgTag(blob);
}

function loadWithImgTag(blob) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const url = URL.createObjectURL(blob);
    const img = new Image();
    img.onload = () => { URL.revokeObjectURL(url); resolve(img); };
    img.onerror = () => { URL.revokeObjectURL(url); reject(new Error('decode')); };
    img.src = url;
  });
}

function canvasToBlob(canvas, type, quality) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    canvas.toBlob((b) => (b ? resolve(b) : reject(new Error('encode'))), type, quality);
  });
}

    If 

    createImageBitmap
    isn't available or fails, the code falls back to a normal 
    img
    element. Modern browsers apply EXIF rotation to 
    img
    elements by default too.

    canvasToBlob
    wraps the callback-based 
    canvas.toBlob()
    in a Promise, so you can use it with 
    await
    .

    Making a Frame Object with a Thumbnail

    A phone photo can be 4000 × 3000 pixels or more. Drawing dozens of those every time the user types a letter would make the preview slow.

    So each frame keeps the original file for the PDF, plus a small JPEG copy (at most 1000 pixels on its longest side) for the frame list and the preview:

    async function makeFrame(file) {
  const pic = await decodeImage(file);
  const w = pic.naturalWidth || pic.width;
  const h = pic.naturalHeight || pic.height;

  // A small copy for the frame list and the preview
  const scale = Math.min(1, THUMB_SIZE / Math.max(w, h));
  const c = document.createElement('canvas');
  c.width = Math.round(w * scale);
  c.height = Math.round(h * scale);
  const ctx = c.getContext('2d');
  ctx.fillStyle = '#ffffff';
  ctx.fillRect(0, 0, c.width, c.height);
  ctx.drawImage(pic, 0, 0, c.width, c.height);
  if (pic.close) pic.close();

  const thumb = await canvasToBlob(c, 'image/jpeg', 0.86);
  return {
    id: 'f' + state.nextId++,
    blob: file, name: file.name, w, h,
    thumb, thumbUrl: URL.createObjectURL(thumb), thumbPic: null,

    Sorting by File Name

    People name their files 

    shot-1.jpg
    , 
    shot-2.jpg

    Adding the Files

    addFiles
    filters out unsupported files, sorts the rest, turns each into a frame and reports anything it skipped:
    async function addFiles(fileList) {
  const files = Array.from(fileList);
  const images = files.filter((f) => ACCEPTED.includes(f.type))
    .sort((a, b) => naturalCompare(a.name, b.name));
  const skipped = files.length - images.length;
  let failed = 0;

  for (let i = 0; i < images.length; i++) {
    els.statusText.textContent = `Reading image ${i + 1} of ${images.length}...`;
    try {
      state.frames.push(await makeFrame(images[i]));
    } catch (err) {
      failed++;
    }
  }

  const notes = [];
  if (skipped) notes.push(`${skipped} file(s) skipped: not JPG, PNG, WebP or GIF`);
  if (failed) notes.push(`${failed} image(s) couldn't be read`);
  els.statusText.textContent = notes.join('. ');

  if (state.frames.length) {
    showWorkspace();
    renderFrameList();
    drawPreview();
    saveDraftSoon();
  }
}

    The images are read one at a time, not all at once with 

    Promise.all
    . Decoding 50 large photos in parallel can run a phone out of memory, and reading them in order also keeps the status message accurate.

    Laying Out a Storyboard Sheet

    This is the heart of the tool. Before drawing anything, the code works out where every box goes, in PDF points from the top-left corner of the sheet.

    Keeping layout separate from drawing means the same layout is used for the small preview on screen and for the 300 dpi PDF. They can't drift apart.

    Calculating the Sheet Size

    // ---------- Layout: where everything goes, in PDF points from the top-left ----------
function sheetSize(o) {
  const [a, b] = PAPERS[o.paper];
  const short = Math.min(a, b);
  const long = Math.max(a, b);
  return o.orient === 'portrait' ? [short, long] : [long, short];
}

    The paper sizes are stored once. Landscape just swaps the short and long sides.

    Laying Out the Frame Boxes

    function computeLayout(o, frameCount) {
  const [W, H] = sheetSize(o);
  const short = Math.min(W, H);
  const margin = short * 0.05;
  const gap = 10;
  const cols = o.layout === 'page' ? 1 : o.cols;
  const rows = o.layout === 'page' ? 1 : o.rows;
  const perSheet = cols * rows;
  const sheets = Math.max(1, Math.ceil(frameCount / perSheet));

  const headH = short * 0.045;              // the title row at the top of each sheet
  const top = margin + headH + margin * 0.5;
  const box = { x: margin, y: top, w: W - 2 * margin, h: H - top - margin };
  const sizeScale = { s: 0.85, m: 1, l: 1.2 }[o.textSize];

  const cellW = (box.w - (cols - 1) * gap) / cols;
  const cellH = (box.h - (rows - 1) * gap) / rows;
  const cells = [];

  for (let r = 0; r < rows; r++) {
    for (let c = 0; c < cols; c++) {
      const x = box.x + c * (cellW + gap);
      const y = box.y + r * (cellH + gap);
      const fs = Math.min(13, Math.max(6.5, cellW * 0.05)) * sizeScale;
      const lh = fs * 1.3;

      if (o.layout === 'notes') {
        // picture on the left, title and ruled lines on the right
        const imgW = Math.min(cellW * 0.5, cellH * 1.6);
        const tx = x + imgW + 8;
        cells.push({ img: { x, y, w: imgW, h: cellH }, text: { x: tx, y, w: x + cellW - tx, h: cellH }, fs, lh, notes: true });
      } else {
        // picture on top, text underneath
        const textH = lh * (1.2 + Number(o.lines)) + fs * 0.6;
        const imgH = Math.max(10, cellH - textH);
        cells.push({ img: { x, y, w: cellW, h: imgH }, text: { x, y: y + imgH + fs * 0.6, w: cellW, h: textH - fs * 0.6 }, fs, lh, strip: o.layout === 'strip' });
      }
    }
  }
  return { W, H, margin, headH, perSheet, sheets, cells };
}

    Here's what happens step by step:

    • The margin is 
      5%
      of the short side, so it scales with the paper.
    • The "One frame per page" layout is a 1 × 1 grid.
    • The number of sheets is the number of frames divided by the frames per sheet, rounded up.
    • A row at the top is kept for the sheet heading.
    • The remaining box is split into equal cells with a fixed gap.
    • The font size depends on the cell width (
      5%
      of it), kept between 
      6.5
      and 
      13
      points, then scaled by the Text size setting.
    • In most layouts, the picture sits on top and the text underneath. The text area is sized for the label line plus the chosen number of description lines.
    • In "Panels with notes", the picture is on the left and the text and ruled lines on the right.

    Each cell ends up with an 

    img
    box and a 
    text
    box, and that's all the drawing code needs to know.

    Fitting an Image Without Stretching It

    A cell is rarely the same shape as the picture. Stretching would distort faces and products, and cropping might cut off what matters. So the picture is scaled to fit inside the box, keeping its proportions, and centered:

    function fitContain(imgW, imgH, box) {
  const s = Math.min(box.w / imgW, box.h / imgH);
  const w = imgW * s;
  const h = imgH * s;
  return { x: box.x + (box.w - w) / 2, y: box.y + (box.h - h) / 2, w, h };
}

    This is the same idea as 

    object-fit: contain
    in CSS. The smaller of the two scale factors wins, so the whole picture always fits.

    Drawing a Sheet on the Canvas

    Wrapping Text into Lines

    Canvas has no automatic line wrapping. 

    fillText
    draws one line, however long it is. So you measure words with 
    measureText
    and build the lines yourself:
    // ---------- Text ----------
function wrapText(ctx, text, maxWidth, maxLines) {
  const words = String(text).trim().split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean);
  const lines = [];
  let line = '';
  for (const word of words) {
    const test = line ? line + ' ' + word : word;
    if (ctx.measureText(test).width <= maxWidth || !line) {
      line = test;
    } else {
      lines.push(line);
      line = word;
    }
  }
  if (line) lines.push(line);

  if (lines.length > maxLines) {
    lines.length = maxLines;
    let last = lines[maxLines - 1];
    while (last && ctx.measureText(last + '…').width > maxWidth) last = last.slice(0, -1);
    lines[maxLines - 1] = last.trimEnd() + '…';
  }
  return lines;
}

    If the description is longer than the lines available, the last line ends with an ellipsis, so the user can see that text was cut.

    Drawing Labels, Titles and Durations

    function frameLabel(o, index) {
  if (o.label === 'number') return String(index + 1);
  if (o.label === 'scene') return `Scene ${index + 1}`;
  if (o.label === 'shot') return `Shot ${index + 1}`;
  return '';
}

function drawFrameText(ctx, o, cell, frame, index, k) {
  const fs = cell.fs * k;
  const lh = cell.lh * k;
  const x = cell.text.x * k;
  const w = cell.text.w * k;
  let y = cell.text.y * k + fs;

  ctx.fillStyle = '#16181b';
  ctx.textBaseline = 'alphabetic';

  // Line 1: label and title on the left, duration on the right
  const dur = formatDuration(frame.dur);
  let room = w;
  if (dur) {
    ctx.font = `${fs}px ${FONTS.mono}`;
    ctx.textAlign = 'right';
    ctx.fillText(dur, x + w, y);
    room -= ctx.measureText(dur).width + fs;
  }
  ctx.textAlign = 'left';
  const head = [frameLabel(o, index), frame.title.trim()].filter(Boolean).join('  ');
  if (head) {
    ctx.font = `bold ${fs}px ${FONTS[o.font]}`;
    ctx.fillText(wrapText(ctx, head, room, 1)[0] || '', x, y);
  }
  y += lh * 1.2;

  // Description, wrapped and cut to the chosen number of lines
  ctx.font = `${fs}px ${FONTS[o.font]}`;
  const maxLines = cell.notes ? Math.floor((cell.text.h * k - lh * 1.2) / lh) : Number(o.lines);
  const lines = frame.desc.trim() ? wrapText(ctx, frame.desc, w, maxLines) : [];
  lines.forEach((line, j) => ctx.fillText(line, x, y + j * lh));

  // Ruled lines for handwritten notes
  if (cell.notes) {
    ctx.strokeStyle = '#c9c6bd';
    ctx.lineWidth = Math.max(1, 0.6 * k);
    const bottom = (cell.text.y + cell.text.h) * k;
    for (let ly = y + lines.length * lh; ly < bottom - 2; ly += lh * 1.25) {
      ctx.beginPath();
      ctx.moveTo(x, ly);
      ctx.lineTo(x + w, ly);
      ctx.stroke();
    }
  }
}

    The parameter 

    k
    is the scale from points to pixels. All positions come from the layout in points and are multiplied by 
    k
    just before drawing. That's what lets the same function draw a 600-pixel preview and a 300 dpi PDF page.

    The duration is drawn first, right-aligned, and the space it takes is subtracted from the room left for the label and title. That way a long title never runs into the duration.

    Drawing the Whole Sheet

    drawSheet
    draws the heading, then each frame on the sheet:
    // ---------- Drawing one sheet ----------
// k turns PDF points into canvas pixels. With mode 'preview' the pictures are
// drawn too; with mode 'overlay' their boxes are left transparent for the PDF.
async function drawSheet(ctx, o, L, sheetIndex, k, mode) {
  const W = L.W * k;
  const H = L.H * k;
  const placed = [];

  ctx.clearRect(0, 0, W, H);
  ctx.fillStyle = '#ffffff';
  ctx.fillRect(0, 0, W, H);

  // Sheet heading: title on the left, total time and sheet number on the right
  const headFs = L.headH * 0.6 * k;
  const base = (L.margin + L.headH * 0.78) * k;
  const total = totalDuration();
  const right = [total ? `Total ${formatDuration(total)}` : '', `Sheet ${sheetIndex + 1} of ${L.sheets}`].filter(Boolean).join(', ');
  ctx.font = `${headFs * 0.72}px ${FONTS.mono}`;
  ctx.fillStyle = '#55585e';
  ctx.textAlign = 'right';
  ctx.fillText(right, W - L.margin * k, base);
  if (state.title) {
    ctx.font = `bold ${headFs}px ${FONTS[o.font]}`;
    ctx.fillStyle = '#16181b';
    ctx.textAlign = 'left';
    ctx.fillText(state.title, L.margin * k, base);
  }
  ctx.strokeStyle = '#c9c6bd';
  ctx.lineWidth = Math.max(1, 0.75 * k);
  ctx.beginPath();
  ctx.moveTo(L.margin * k, (L.margin + L.headH) * k);
  ctx.lineTo(W - L.margin * k, (L.margin + L.headH) * k);
  ctx.stroke();

  const start = sheetIndex * L.perSheet;
  const items = state.frames.slice(start, start + L.perSheet);

  for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i++) {
    const cell = L.cells[i];
    const frame = items[i];

    // Film strip: a dark band with sprocket holes behind the picture
    if (cell.strip) {
      const b = cell.img;
      const hole = b.h * 0.08;
      ctx.fillStyle = '#16181b';
      ctx.fillRect(b.x * k, b.y * k, b.w * k, b.h * k);
      ctx.fillStyle = '#ffffff';
      for (let hx = b.x + hole; hx + hole < b.x + b.w; hx += hole * 2) {
        ctx.fillRect(hx * k, (b.y + hole * 0.3) * k, hole * k, hole * 0.5 * k);
        ctx.fillRect(hx * k, (b.y + b.h - hole * 0.8) * k, hole * k, hole * 0.5 * k);
      }
    }

    const area = cell.strip
      ? { x: cell.img.x, y: cell.img.y + cell.img.h * 0.12, w: cell.img.w, h: cell.img.h * 0.76 }
      : cell.img;
    const rect = fitContain(frame.w, frame.h, area);
    placed.push({ frame, rect });

    const px = { x: Math.round(rect.x * k), y: Math.round(rect.y * k), w: Math.round(rect.w * k), h: Math.round(rect.h * k) };
    if (mode === 'overlay') {
      ctx.clearRect(px.x, px.y, px.w, px.h);
    } else {
      if (!frame.thumbPic) frame.thumbPic = await decodeImage(frame.thumb);
      ctx.drawImage(frame.thumbPic, px.x, px.y, px.w, px.h);
    }
    if (!cell.strip) {
      ctx.strokeStyle = '#16181b';
      ctx.lineWidth = Math.max(1, 0.9 * k);
      ctx.strokeRect(cell.img.x * k, cell.img.y * k, cell.img.w * k, cell.img.h * k);
    }
    drawFrameText(ctx, o, cell, frame, start + i, k);
  }
  return placed;
}

    The 

    mode
    parameter is the important trick here:
    • In 
      'preview'
      mode, the pictures are drawn from the thumbnails.
    • In 
      'overlay'
      mode, the picture areas are cleared to transparent, and the function returns where each picture should go.

    You'll see why in the PDF section. For the film strip, the dark band and the sprocket holes are drawn first, and the picture sits in the middle of the band.

    Previewing the Sheets

    The preview draws the current sheet at the canvas's on-screen width, multiplied by the device pixel ratio so it stays sharp on high-density screens:

let previewTimer = null;

  previewTimer = setTimeout(drawPreview, 150);

async function drawPreview() {
  if (!state.frames.length) return;
  const o = state.opts;
  const L = computeLayout(o, state.frames.length);
  state.sheet = Math.min(state.sheet, L.sheets - 1);

  // Draw at the canvas's on-screen width, sharp on high-density screens
  const cssWidth = els.canvas.clientWidth || 600;
  const k = (cssWidth * Math.min(2, window.devicePixelRatio || 1)) / L.W;
  els.canvas.width = Math.round(L.W * k);
  els.canvas.height = Math.round(L.H * k);
  await drawSheet(els.canvas.getContext('2d'), o, L, state.sheet, k, 'preview');

  els.sheetInfo.textContent = `Sheet ${state.sheet + 1} of ${L.sheets}`;
  els.prevBtn.disabled = state.sheet === 0;
  els.nextBtn.disabled = state.sheet >= L.sheets - 1;
}

els.nextBtn.addEventListener('click', () => { state.sheet++; drawPreview(); });

    Saving a Draft with IndexedDB

    Writing descriptions for 30 frames takes time. Losing that work to an accidental reload is frustrating, so the tool saves a draft as the user works.

    localStorage
    won't do here. It only stores strings, and most browsers limit it to about 5 MB, which is less than two phone photos. IndexedDB can store 
    Blob
    objects directly and allows far more space.

    Opening the Database

    // ---------- Draft in IndexedDB ----------
const DB_NAME = 'image-storyboard';
let dbPromise = null;

function openDb() {
  if (!dbPromise) {
    dbPromise = new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
      const req = indexedDB.open(DB_NAME, 1);
      req.onupgradeneeded = () => req.result.createObjectStore('drafts');
      req.onsuccess = () => resolve(req.result);
      req.onerror = () => reject(req.error);
    });
  }
  return dbPromise;
}

async function dbRun(mode, work) {
  const db = await openDb();
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const tx = db.transaction('drafts', mode);
    const result = work(tx.objectStore('drafts'));
    tx.oncomplete = () => resolve(result && result.result);
    tx.onerror = () => reject(tx.error);
  });
}


    dbRun
    wraps a transaction in a Promise. It resolves when the transaction completes, so a write is only reported as done once it's actually stored.

    Saving the Draft

    let saveTimer = null;
function saveDraftSoon() {
  clearTimeout(saveTimer);
  saveTimer = setTimeout(saveDraft, 800);
}

function saveDraft() {
  const draft = {
    title: state.title,
    savedAt: Date.now(),
    frames: state.frames.map(({ blob, name, title, desc, dur }) => ({ blob, name, title, desc, dur })),
  };
  return dbRun('readwrite', (store) => store.put(draft, 'current')).catch(() => {
    els.resultText.textContent = 'This browser could not save a draft. Download the PDF before closing the tab.';
  });
}

    The draft stores the original image files as Blobs, along with the text the user typed. Thumbnails and object URLs aren't stored, because they can be made again from the files.

    saveDraftSoon
    waits until the user pauses for 800 ms, so typing a description doesn't write to the database on every key press.

    If saving fails, for example in a private window with storage blocked, the tool tells the user to download the PDF before closing the tab instead of failing silently.

    Restoring the Draft

    When the page loads, the tool checks for a draft and offers to restore it:

  try {
    const draft = await dbRun('readonly', (store) => store.get('current'));
    if (!draft || !draft.frames.length) return;
    els.draftText.textContent = `You have a saved storyboard with ${draft.frames.length} frames.`;
    els.draftBar.hidden = false;
  } catch (err) { /* no storage: nothing to restore */ }
}

els.restoreBtn.addEventListener('click', async () => {
  const draft = await dbRun('readonly', (store) => store.get('current'));
  for (const saved of draft.frames) {
    const file = new File([saved.blob], saved.name, { type: saved.blob.type });
    const frame = await makeFrame(file);
    Object.assign(frame, { title: saved.title, desc: saved.desc, dur: saved.dur });
    state.frames.push(frame);
  }
  state.title = draft.title || '';
  els.boardTitle.value = state.title;
  showWorkspace();
  renderFrameList();
  drawPreview();
});

els.discardBtn.addEventListener('click', () => {
  dbRun('readwrite', (store) => store.delete('current'));
  els.draftBar.hidden = true;
});

    Each saved Blob goes back through 

    makeFrame
    , so restored frames get fresh thumbnails, and then the saved text is copied onto them.

    Generating the PDF with PDF-lib

    The simplest way to make the PDF would be to draw each whole sheet on a canvas, with the pictures, and put that canvas in the PDF as one image. It works, but it forces a choice:

    • Save it as PNG and the photos make the file huge.
    • Save it as JPEG and the text and thin lines get blurry edges.

    So the tool uses two layers on each page:

    • Pictures as JPEG, each at the resolution the user chose, placed exactly in its box
    • Text, labels and lines as one transparent PNG at 300 dpi, covering the whole page on top

    JPEG is good for photos, and PNG keeps text sharp. This is why 

    drawSheet
    has the 
    'overlay'
    mode that leaves holes where the pictures go.

    Turning Each Picture into a JPEG

    // ---------- Making the PDF ----------
async function imageAsJpeg(frame, widthPx, heightPx) {
  const pic = await decodeImage(frame.blob);
  const c = document.createElement('canvas');
  c.width = Math.max(1, Math.round(widthPx));
  c.height = Math.max(1, Math.round(heightPx));
  const ctx = c.getContext('2d');
  ctx.fillStyle = '#ffffff';              // transparent PNGs get a white background
  ctx.fillRect(0, 0, c.width, c.height);
  ctx.imageSmoothingQuality = 'high';
  ctx.drawImage(pic, 0, 0, c.width, c.height);
  if (pic.close) pic.close();
  const blob = await canvasToBlob(c, 'image/jpeg', 0.9);
  return new Uint8Array(await blob.arrayBuffer());
}

    The picture is decoded again from the original file, not from the thumbnail, so the PDF has full quality.

    Building the Pages

    async function buildPdf() {
  const { PDFDocument } = PDFLib;
  const o = state.opts;
  const L = computeLayout(o, state.frames.length);
  const dpi = Number(els.quality.value);
  const k = 300 / 72;                         // text layer at 300 dpi

  const pdf = await PDFDocument.create();
  for (let s = 0; s < L.sheets; s++) {
    els.resultText.textContent = `Making sheet ${s + 1} of ${L.sheets}...`;
    const page = pdf.addPage([L.W, L.H]);

    // 1. Text, labels and lines on a canvas, with holes where the pictures go
    const c = document.createElement('canvas');
    c.width = Math.round(L.W * k);
    c.height = Math.round(L.H * k);
    const placed = await drawSheet(c.getContext('2d'), o, L, s, k, 'overlay');

    // 2. Each picture as a JPEG at the chosen resolution, placed in its hole
    for (const { frame, rect } of placed) {
      const scale = Math.min(1, (rect.w * dpi / 72) / frame.w);
      const jpg = await pdf.embedJpg(await imageAsJpeg(frame, frame.w * scale, frame.h * scale));
      // PDF y runs from the bottom of the page, the canvas y from the top
      page.drawImage(jpg, { x: rect.x, y: L.H - rect.y - rect.h, width: rect.w, height: rect.h });
    }

    // 3. The text layer on top, as one transparent PNG covering the page
    const pngBlob = await canvasToBlob(c, 'image/png');
    const png = await pdf.embedPng(new Uint8Array(await pngBlob.arrayBuffer()));
    page.drawImage(png, { x: 0, y: 0, width: L.W, height: L.H });
    c.width = 1;                               // free the canvas memory
  }

  pdf.setTitle(state.title || 'Storyboard');
  return pdf.save();
}

    Here's what happens on each page:

    • addPage([L.W, L.H])
      creates a page in points, the same units as the layout.
    • The text layer is drawn at 
      k = 300 / 72
      , which is 300 pixels per inch.
    • Each picture is resized to the chosen dpi for the size it has on the page. A 4000-pixel photo shown 2 inches wide only needs 600 pixels at 300 dpi, so the file stays small. 
      Math.min(1, ...)
      makes sure small pictures are never enlarged.
    • The pictures are drawn first, then the transparent PNG on top of them.

    Note the y coordinate: 

    L.H - rect.y - rect.h
    . The layout and the canvas measure y from the top of the page, but PDF measures y from the bottom. Forgetting this flip puts every picture upside down in the page, the classic PDF-lib mistake.

    Setting 

    c.width = 1
    after use frees the canvas memory right away, which matters on phones when there are many sheets.

    Renaming and Downloading

    The file name comes from a text field, cleaned of characters that aren't allowed in file names:

    // ---------- Download ----------
function cleanFileName(name) {
  const n = name.trim().replace(/\.pdf$/i, '').replace(/[\\/:*?"<>|]+/g, '-');
  return (n || 'storyboard') + '.pdf';
}

function formatSize(bytes) {
  return bytes < 1024 * 1024 ? `${Math.round(bytes / 1024)} KB` : `${(bytes / 1024 / 1024).toFixed(1)} MB`;
}

els.downloadBtn.addEventListener('click', async () => {
  if (!state.frames.length) return;
  els.downloadBtn.disabled = true;
  try {
    const bytes = await buildPdf();
    const name = cleanFileName(els.fileName.value);
    const url = URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([bytes], { type: 'application/pdf' }));
    const a = document.createElement('a');
    a.href = url;
    a.download = name;
    a.click();
    setTimeout(() => URL.revokeObjectURL(url), 60000);
    els.resultText.textContent = `Saved ${name} (${formatSize(bytes.length)}).`;
  } catch (err) {
    console.error(err);
    els.resultText.textContent = 'The PDF could not be made. Try fewer images or the 150 dpi setting.';
  } finally {
    els.downloadBtn.disabled = false;
  }
});

    The object URL is revoked after a minute, which is long enough for the download to start and frees the memory afterwards. The button is disabled while the PDF is being made, so a double click can't start two exports.

    Finally, "Start over" clears the state, the draft and the object URLs. The last two lines of the file read the default settings and check for a saved draft when the page loads:

    // ---------- Start over ----------
els.resetBtn.addEventListener('click', () => {
  clearTimeout(saveTimer);
  state.frames.forEach((f) => URL.revokeObjectURL(f.thumbUrl));
  state.frames = [];
  state.title = '';
  state.sheet = 0;
  state.lastDeleted = null;
  els.boardTitle.value = '';
  els.undoBtn.hidden = true;
  els.resultText.textContent = '';
  els.workspace.hidden = true;
  els.uploadArea.hidden = false;
  dbRun('readwrite', (store) => store.delete('current')).catch(() => {});
});

readSettings();
checkDraft();

    Demo: How the Image Storyboard Tool Works

    Here's the whole workflow in the finished tool.

    Step 1: Add Your Images

    Drop a folder's worth of images on the page or click Select images. They're sorted by file name, so 

    shot-1
    , 
    shot-2
    … 
    shot-10
    land in the right order.

    Step 2: Put the Frames in Order

    Drag a thumbnail onto another card, or use the Up and Down buttons.

    Step 3: Write the Script

    Give each frame a title, a description and a duration. The total running time updates as you type.

    Step 4: Choose a Layout

    Pick one frame per page, a grid, panels with notes or a film strip, then set the paper size and orientation.

    Step 5: Check the Preview

    Use Previous and Next to look at every sheet before you download.

    Step 6: Download the PDF

    Type a file name, choose the image quality and click Download PDF.

    Performance Tips

    Use thumbnails for everything on screen. The preview redraws often, while the user types and changes settings. Drawing 1000-pixel thumbnails instead of full photos keeps it fast. Only the PDF export touches the original files.

    Decode thumbnails once. In 

    drawSheet
    , each frame keeps its decoded thumbnail in 
    frame.thumbPic
    , so switching sheets doesn't decode the same image again.

    Process images one at a time. Reading or exporting dozens of large photos with 

    Promise.all
    can use more memory than a phone has. A simple 
    for
    loop with 
    await
    keeps only one large image in memory at a time.

    Size pictures for the page, not the camera. A picture's pixel size in the PDF should depend on how big it is on the page and the chosen dpi. That one line in 

    buildPdf
    is often the difference between a 3 MB file and a 60 MB file.

    Release memory as you go. Call 

    close()
    on an 
    ImageBitmap
    when you're done with it, set used canvases to 
    width = 1
    , and revoke object URLs you no longer need.

    Common Mistakes

    Sideways phone photos. If you read an image's size or draw it without applying EXIF orientation, portrait photos come out landscape. Use 

    createImageBitmap(blob, { imageOrientation: 'from-image' })
    .

    Stretched pictures. Drawing an image straight into a cell with 

    drawImage(img, x, y, cellW, cellH)
    stretches it. Always fit it with a "contain" calculation like 
    fitContain
    first.

    Wrong order of files. The order files arrive from a file picker or a drop isn't guaranteed. Sort them yourself, and use a numeric sort so 

    shot-10
    comes after 
    shot-9
    .

    Forgetting to flip the y axis. Canvas y goes down from the top, PDF y goes up from the bottom. Convert with 

    pageHeight - y - height
    when placing anything with PDF-lib.

    Black backgrounds on transparent PNGs. JPEG has no transparency. Fill the canvas with white before drawing a PNG you'll save as JPEG.

    Rebuilding the list while the user types. Re-rendering inputs on every key press moves the cursor and loses focus. Update the state from the 

    input
    event and only rebuild the list when the order changes.

    Canvases that are too large. Browsers limit canvas size, and phones have tight limits. An A3 page at 300 dpi is about 4960 × 3508 pixels, which is fine, but don't multiply that by the device pixel ratio as well.

    Conclusion

    In this tutorial, you built a browser-based tool that turns a set of images into storyboard sheets and a print-ready PDF.

    You learned how to apply phone photo rotation with 

    createImageBitmap
    , sort file names numerically, keep layout math in PDF points so the preview and the PDF always match, wrap text on a canvas, save a draft of images and text in IndexedDB, and build a two-layer PDF with sharp text and compact photos using PDF-lib.

    All of it runs locally in the browser, so the images stay on the user's device.

    You can try the full version of this tool, with more options such as sheet colors, a handwritten font, one PDF per frame and PNG export, at Image Storyboard to PDF.

entries.content:
AI coding agents such as Codex read your codebase, edit multiple files, and run commands and tests while they work through larger tasks with you. In Codex, an AGENTS.md file holds persistent instructions for a project, and config.toml holds the agent's configuration.

We just published a course on the freeCodeCamp.org YouTube channel that will teach you how to get reliable results from a coding agent by giving it the right context, planning the work, controlling its permissions, and verifying every change. This course is taught by Tom Chant, Head of Education at Scrimba.

You'll work through realistic tasks, including challenges on skills, characterization tests, and config.toml. The course is aimed at experienced developers adding AI to their workflow and at non-coders who want to build software with AI help. You can also study it interactively on Scrimba.

In this course, you will learn:

  • Prompting & Project Setup

    How to write effective prompts and comment prompts for a coding agent, then initialize a project and use multiple AGENTS.md files.
  • Plan Mode & Skills

    How to break larger development tasks down with Plan Mode and extend a coding agent with skills.
  • Testing Agent Changes

    How to verify an agent's changes with characterization tests and test-driven development (TDD), and which testing pitfalls to look out for.
  • Git & Secrets

    How to use Git safely alongside a coding agent and keep API keys, credentials, and other secrets safe.
  • Context, Permissions & config.toml

    How to use the VS Code Codex extension, manage context, control what an agent can access and change, and configure it with config.toml.
  • MCP & shadcn

    How to connect agents to external tools with the Model Context Protocol (MCP), including shadcn.

Watch the full course on the freeCodeCamp.org YouTube channel (2-hour watch).
